topic: Worry, contrast avoidance and intolerance of uncertainty
text:
Worry is often seen as a habit of thinking too much that people simply need to switch off. The research suggests something more useful to hold in mind: for many people, worry may be doing a job.

The contrast avoidance model, developed by Michelle Newman and colleagues, proposes that some people find a sharp shift from feeling okay to feeling bad especially hard to bear. Worry keeps them braced, so if something does go wrong, the drop feels smaller. If nothing goes wrong, the relief that follows can strengthen the belief that worrying helped, which may keep it going.

In a 2023 study of more than 1,400 university students, those who screened positive for generalised anxiety, depression or social anxiety all reported more discomfort with these sudden emotional shifts than those who did not. The authors suggest this may be a shared feature across all three.

A related thread is intolerance of uncertainty, a tendency to find not knowing hard to endure. A 2019 meta-analysis led by researchers at Curtin University in Perth pooled 181 studies with more than 52,000 participants and found it was consistently linked with symptoms of anxiety, depression, obsessive compulsive difficulties and eating disorders.

A 2026 experiment with 154 adults diagnosed with anxiety or obsessive compulsive disorders found that when a brief task shifted how uncomfortable people felt with uncertainty in the moment, that shift was linked with how stuck they felt on two real personal decisions. The authors describe this as a tentative finding.

What this might mean in practice, whatever your role:
• Notice when worry is framed as protection, such as "if I expect the worst, I will not be let down". This may be the pattern at work rather than simple overthinking.
• Ask with curiosity what worrying does for the person, and notice when everyday decisions feel stuck, as difficulty with not knowing may sit underneath.
• When worry, low mood or indecision is affecting daily life, talk with the person about involving their GP or psychologist so the pattern can be properly assessed.

Where the evidence stops:
• The 2023 study captured one point in time, used self-report screening and drew on students, so it cannot show cause and may not reflect the wider community.
• The meta-analysis also pooled studies measured at one point in time, so it shows a link, not that intolerance of uncertainty causes symptoms.
• The 2026 experiment found only an indirect effect in a mixed diagnostic group, and the authors note more robust approaches are needed.

Follow along for more research like this.

Key sources:
• Newman et al., 2023: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.janxdis.2022.102662
• McEvoy et al., 2019: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cpr.2019.101778
• Appel et al., 2026: https://doi.org/10.1002/jclp.70160
